So I decided to do some digging into this case, and found some useful information:

And here's Sixmile Creek, according to Google Maps: https://www.google.com/maps/place/Fire+Department/@41.2497659,-110.4262968,16z/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x8751aa6465265771:0xf133d018b447c088!6m1!1e1

Ironically enough, it's not six miles. Maybe it was when Wyoming was getting more rain it would stretch that far, but not now.

I don't know the guy's address, but the satellite view shows a nice big pond here: http://i.imgur.com/5Iua7ZX.jpg (Remember, the guy's been fighting the EPA since 2014. Satellite photos get updated more often than that.)

And gosh, but that pond has just the same diving board and gravel driveway as the one photographed by James Young for their article in the Deseret News!

So just how big is this thing? I used Google's distance measurement tool to get a rough approximation. 650 feet around - that translates into about 33,500 square feet of "stock tank" on his property.

So it's pretty fair to say at this point that we're not talking about a stock tank. He's got a diving board on the thing, it's for recreation.

Here's some more information, courtesy of a nicely detailed article in the Wyoming News:

“I think they’re trying to gain jurisdiction,” Johnson said. “They’re trying to see if they can run over me, and then they will get into everyone’s irrigation ditch and stock ponds throughout not only Wyoming, but the United States."

That's the quote from this guy. I can't say if it's accurate or not, but I can say that the whole area's been pretty thirsty for water these last 5 years or so. Why would an environmental agency not be interested? And, just a side note - building yourself a pond during a drought is pretty dickish.

...the EPA, which sent Johnson a compliance order in January 2014 instructing him to remove the stock pond or face $37,500 in fines for every day he refused to do so.

So this $16 MILLION pricetag is a little overblown. The per-day fine is as an incentive to get the thing taken down, and the guy decided to thumb his nose at them since 2014. What did he think they'd do, just stop counting?

Further, the EPA isn't trying to shake this guy down for money. When our city had to cite some businesses for water discharge, we even let them put the cost of the fines toward the RO systems they used to get back in compliance. They'll probably pursue him for it at this point, but just out of spite for taking them to court. The EPA in my area doesn't fuck around.

Johnson has retained the services of the Pacific Legal Foundation, a California-based public interest law firm and self-described watchdog organization that specializes in arguing for limited government, property rights, individual rights and "a balanced approach to environmental protection," according to its website.

Somebody's taking this up as an example case. Anyone care to do some research into Pacific Legal Foundation?

I can think of some rich fucks who'd love to have a "stock tank" in their backyard, complete with a diving board and swim-up bar.

Wood said Johnson's pond has, in fact, proven environmentally beneficial, creating new habitat for fish, wildlife and migratory birds. Further, he said independent lab tests have shown the water flowing out of the pond is three times cleaner than the water entering it, and the amount of suspended solids in the pond are 41 times smaller than in the nearest navigable waterway, the Green River.

This is the same lawyer who earlier referred to the $16 million fine as "approaching $20 million." Expect this man to stretch every definition of the truth. "Habitat for fish" probably means some decorative koi. "Migratory birds" is equally bullshit.

As far as the independent lab tests, that's a misdirect. Any well-kept pond is going to drop its phosphorus and TSS, as it's basically a settling tank. Why is he bringing this up? The EPA didn't go after the stock tank because it was dirty.

"It's incredibly ironic that the agency that's right now in hot water for having dumped 3 million gallons of toxic water into a river is wasting its time and resources going after Andy for doing something that's actually good for the environment," Wood said.

Ah, gotta get a nice political jab in there. This explains the mention of water quality, and is quite a good misdirect by the lawyer. Now suddenly we're not talking about the guy's water usage - we're talking about cleanliness - something much easier for them to defend.

Along with Wood, Johnson is receiving local representation from attorneys Dan Frank of Frank Law Office and Karen Budd-Falen with Budd-Falen Law Offices. All three offices are helping Johnson free of charge.

Money doesn't come from nowhere, and lawyers hardly ever work for free. Either they're doing this for the publicity, or because there are rich clients out there somewhere who want to turn this "stock tank" definition into a loophole for their own properties.

Either that, or there's something larger going on with a dedicated effort to attack the EPA. I'm not entirely sure on that one, but this certainly smells fishy.
